claim: 43 human participants underwent fMRI while performing an observational learning task.
source: 43 human participants underwent fMRI while performing an observational learning (OL) task (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and participant count.

claim: Participants observed agents make repeated binary choices between pairs of slot machines sampled from a pool of three slot machines.
source: 43 human participants underwent fMRI while performing an observational learning (OL) task (Figure 1A), in which on each of two sessions they observed an agent make repeated binary choices between pairs of slot machines, sampled by the computer from a pool of three slot machines.
evidence: This describes the experimental task structure directly stated in the manuscript.

claim: Each slot machine delivered one of three different food items as a prize on each trial.
source: Participants were instructed that each of the slot machines would on each trial deliver one of three different food items as a prize.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design.

claim: Food items were selected to differ in their subjective value to the participant.
source: These food items were selected to differ in their subjective value to the participant (one was a preferred food item, another middle ranked, and another least preferred, drawn from an initial list of 10 food items that were earlier ranked for preference).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for food item selection.

claim: Food items were delivered with differing but fixed probabilities across sessions.
source: These items were delivered with differing (but fixed across session) probabilities.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the probability structure of the task.

claim: Participants never saw any outcomes of the slot machines.
source: The critical feature of this paradigm is that participants never got to see any outcomes of the slot machines while participants understood that the agents did receive the outcomes.
evidence: This is a key experimental design feature explicitly stated.

claim: Participants understood that the agents received the outcomes.
source: The critical feature of this paradigm is that participants never got to see any outcomes of the slot machines while participants understood that the agents did receive the outcomes.
evidence: This describes what participants were told about the task.

claim: On one-third of trials, participants themselves made choices between the same slot machines.
source: Occasionally (1/3 of trials), the participants themselves were presented with the same slot machines as those played by the agents, and they had to make a choice.
evidence: This describes the trial structure of the experiment.

claim: One agent had similar food preferences to the participant while the other agent had dissimilar food preferences.
source: One agent had similar food preferences to the participant while the other agent had dissimilar food preferences.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of agent preferences.

claim: Each participant correctly identified the preference rankings for each agent over the foods.
source: Each participant correctly identified the preference rankings for each agent over the foods, as well as correctly classifying the agents as similar or dissimilar to themselves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the preference learning phase.

claim: Participants correctly classified the agents as similar or dissimilar to themselves.
source: Each participant correctly identified the preference rankings for each agent over the foods, as well as correctly classifying the agents as similar or dissimilar to themselves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the preference learning phase.

claim: Participants' choice ratios were generally in line with the agents' choice ratios.
source: Spearman's rank correlation coefficients between participants' choices in self-referential space and agent choices in agent-space, revealed that participants' choice ratios were generally in line with the agents': rs_sim = 0.7 (similar condition), rs_dis = 0.6 (dissimilar condition; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: Participants succeeded in learning to choose the slot machine with the highest likelihood of a preferred outcome.
source: These correlations also provide evidence that participants succeeded in learning to choose the slot machine with the highest likelihood of a preferred outcome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation results.

claim: Participants performed significantly worse overall in the dissimilar condition compared to the similar condition.
source: Indeed, participants performed significantly worse overall in the dissimilar condition compared to the similar (after Fisher transform: one-tailed p=0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing performance across conditions.

claim: Participants performed equally well in choosing their 'best' slot machine in both similar and dissimilar conditions.
source: Here we found that although participants performed equally well in choosing their 'best' slot machine in both similar and dissimilar conditions (t-test between similar and dissimilar choice ratios: P>0.6)
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: The worst slot machine was picked more often in the dissimilar condition than in the similar condition.
source: the worst slot machine was picked more often in the dissimilar condition than in the similar (P<0.05)
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: The mid-ranking machine was chosen significantly less often in the dissimilar condition compared to the similar condition.
source: the mid-ranking machine was chosen significantly less often in the dissimilar condition compared to the similar (P<0.05, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: The non-symmetrical choice difference between observer and agent alludes to a more sophisticated strategy than simple imitation behavior.
source: This non-symmetrical choice difference between observer and agent, that is, equal performance for the best, but not simply reversed for the mid and worst machines, alludes to a more sophisticated strategy than simple imitation behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral pattern observed.

claim: Inverse RL was found to outperform Imitation RL overall.
source: Out of all tested models, inverse RL was found to outperform Imitation RL overall (Figure 2A) and in almost all individual subjects (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian Model Selection analysis.

claim: Inverse RL outperformed Imitation RL in almost all individual subjects.
source: Out of all tested models, inverse RL was found to outperform Imitation RL overall (Figure 2A) and in almost all individual subjects (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian Model Selection analysis.

claim: The inverse RL model outperformed other candidate algorithms including counterfactual imitation RL and preference-learning algorithms.
source: The model similarly also outperformed the other candidate algorithms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: The choices estimated by the inverse RL model match participants' behavior very well.
source: The choices estimated by the inverse RL model match participants' behavior very well when plotting model predictions against participants' actual (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from model validation analysis.

claim: The two main competing models (inverse RL and imitation RL) are not confused and make different predictions.
source: However this comparison framework shows that our main models are indeed not confused, and hence make different predictions (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from confusion matrix analysis.

claim: The behavior that discriminates the model predictions the most is with regard to participants' behavior to the middle preferred slot machine when learning from the dissimilar other.
source: When comparing model choice predictions and participant choice ratios. While both imitation RL and inverse RL do quite reasonably in predicting choices for the most and least preferred slot machine, we found that the behavior that discriminates the model predictions the most is with regard to participants' behavior to the middle preferred slot machine when learning from the dissimilar other.
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: Variation in selection of the middle preferred slot machine was much more effectively captured by inverse RL compared to imitation RL.
source: There was considerable variation across individuals in the selection of the middle preferred slot machine: this variation was much more effectively captured by inverse RL compared to imitation RL (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis.

claim: A significant cluster in the dmPFC correlated positively with the agent's value signals in both the similar and dissimilar conditions.
source: We found a significant cluster in the dmPFC (Figure 3A; peak x = 0, y = 40, z = 40, whole brain cluster corrected threshold of FWE at p<0.05 with a height threshold of p<0.001) correlating positively with the agent's value signals in the similar condition, as well as positively with the agent's value signals in the dissimilar condition (Figure 3B, parameter estimates extracted via a leave-one-out approach to avoid a non-independence bias [Esterman et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is a result from fMRI analysis with statistical thresholding.

claim: No statistical difference was found between conditions in dmPFC value signal correlations.
source: Further, no statistical difference was found between conditions (t-test p>0.5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from fMRI data analysis.

claim: Expected value signals for outcomes are represented in agent-referential preference space.
source: These results indicate that expected value signals for outcomes are represented in agent-referential preference space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: The anterior part of dmPFC is much more likely to encode inverse RL computations compared to imitation RL.
source: Our results show that the anterior part of the dorsomedial cluster is much more likely to be engaged in computing expectations derived from the inverse RL model, compared to the imitation RL (Figure 3C, exceedance probability threshold of p>0.95 for inverse RL).
evidence: This is a result from Bayesian Model Selection analysis on fMRI data.

claim: Significant correlations with the entropy reduction signal were found in TPJ/pSTS in both similar and dissimilar conditions.
source: We found significant correlations with the entropy reduction signal in both similar and dissimilar conditions, in TPJ/pSTS (whole brain cluster corrected threshold of FWE at p<0.05 with a height threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from fMRI analysis with statistical thresholding.

claim: Significant correlations with the learning signal were found in pre-SMA and dorsal striatum.
source: In addition we found significant correlations with this learning signal in several other brain regions including the pre-SMA and dorsal striatum (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from fMRI analysis.

claim: No significant difference in the representation of updating signals was found between the similar and dissimilar conditions.
source: Furthermore no significant difference in the representation of updating signals was found between the similar and dissimilar conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical result from fMRI data analysis.

claim: Learning from similar and dissimilar others involves overlapping computational mechanisms involving the same brain regions.
source: The findings suggest that learning from similar and dissimilar others involves overlapping computational mechanisms involving the same brain regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: No cluster survived the predefined threshold for neural correlations with the prediction error signal from the imitation RL model.
source: We also looked at the neural correlations with the prediction error signal from the imitation RL model in a separate GLM. However no cluster survived the predefined threshold (whole brain cluster corrected threshold of FWE at p<0.05 with a height threshold of p<0.001).
evidence: This is a negative result from fMRI analysis.

claim: A significant correlation was found between the social information integration index and the extent to which dmPFC represented learned values for the dissimilar other.
source: We found a significant correlation between this social information integration index (SI index, Materials and methods) and the extent to which dmPFC represented learned values for the dissimilar other (Figure 5A, p<0.01, R = 0.39).
evidence: This is a statistical result from brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: No significant correlation was found between the social information integration index and activity in the TPJ/pSTS.
source: For comparison, we performed the same correlation against activity in the TPJ/pSTS, and we found no such significant correlation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a negative result from brain-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: Participants implemented inverse RL as opposed to a simple imitation strategy.
source: Using formal model comparison, we found that participants implemented inverse RL as opposed to a simple imitation strategy, in which the actions of the other agent are copied instead of inferring the underlying reward structure of the decision problem.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Anterior dorsomedial prefrontal cortex encoded inferences about action-values within the value space of the agent as opposed to that of the observer.
source: Our computational fMRI analysis revealed that anterior dorsomedial prefrontal cortex encoded inferences about action-values within the value space of the agent as opposed to that of the observer, demonstrating that inverse RL is an abstract cognitive process divorceable from the values and concerns of the observer him/herself.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Inverse RL is an abstract cognitive process divorceable from the values and concerns of the observer.
source: Our computational fMRI analysis revealed that anterior dorsomedial prefrontal cortex encoded inferences about action-values within the value space of the agent as opposed to that of the observer, demonstrating that inverse RL is an abstract cognitive process divorceable from the values and concerns of the observer him/herself.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: In imitation learning, an individual simply learns about the actions of an observed agent by learning to copy the agent's behavior.
source: When learning through observing others' actions, two major strategies have been proposed: in imitation learning, an individual simply learns about the actions of an observed agent, in essence by learning to copy the agent's behavior.
evidence: This is a definition of imitation learning from the literature.

claim: In inverse reinforcement-learning, the observer uses the agent's actions to infer the hidden or unobservable properties of the environment.
source: An alternative strategy called inverse reinforcement-learning (inverse RL) is to use the agent's actions to infer the hidden or unobservable properties of the environment, such as the reward outcomes available for pursuing particular actions.
evidence: This is a definition of inverse RL from the literature.

claim: In imitation learning, the observer learns nothing about the structure of the environment other than the action tendencies of the agents they observe.
source: While in imitation learning, the observer learns nothing about the structure of the environment other than the action tendencies of the agents they observe, in inverse RL the observer has acquired knowledge of the world which becomes ultimately abstracted from the actions of the agent they observe.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction between the two learning strategies.

claim: In inverse RL, the observer has acquired knowledge of the world which becomes ultimately abstracted from the actions of the agent they observe.
source: While in imitation learning, the observer learns nothing about the structure of the environment other than the action tendencies of the agents they observe, in inverse RL the observer has acquired knowledge of the world which becomes ultimately abstracted from the actions of the agent they observe.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction between the two learning strategies.

claim: Inverse RL offers greater flexibility to learn from diverse agents, even under the situation where the agent has very distinct preferences or goals to that observer.
source: Although imitation learning can work well under a number of situations, particularly where the agent can be assumed to have similar preferences to the observer, inverse RL offers greater flexibility to learn from diverse agents, even under the situation where the agent has very distinct preferences or goals to that observer.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the advantages of inverse RL.

claim: The computational framework of inverse RL was originally developed by researchers in the artificial intelligence community.
source: The computational framework of inverse RL was originally developed by researchers in the artificial intelligence community (Ng and Russell, 2000; Abbeel and Ng, 2004).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citations.

claim: Observational learning has recently been formalized as an inverse problem, where observed behavior is used to infer the hidden structure at the root of that behavior under the assumption that observed choices are goal-directed.
source: Observational learning has recently been formalized as an inverse problem, where observed behavior is used to infer the hidden structure at the root of that behavior under the assumption that observed choices are goal-directed (Baker et al., 2009, Baker et al., 2011; Goodman et al., 2009; Shafto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about recent computational modeling work supported by citations.

claim: Recent computational modeling work has focused on how humans create an understanding of other's preferences and the similarity to one's own past choices, to guide future behavior.
source: Recent computational modeling work has focused on how humans create an understanding of other's preferences and the similarity to one's own past choices, to guide future behavior (Gershman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a claim about recent research supported by a citation.

claim: Computing abstract social inferences has been characterized as emerging already in early infancy.
source: Computing abstract social inferences has been characterized as emerging already in early infancy (Lucas et al., 2009; Jara-Ettinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a claim about developmental research supported by citations.

claim: There is empirical evidence that subjective preferences emerge in toddlers as early as 16 to 18 months.
source: There is empirical evidence that subjective preferences emerge in toddlers as early as 16 to 18 months (Repacholi and Gopnik, 1997; Ma and Xu, 2011)
evidence: This is a claim about developmental research supported by citations.

claim: By the age of three children use inferences about social preferences to guide their own decisions.
source: by the age of three children use inferences about social preferences to guide their own decisions (Fawcett and Markson, 2010).
evidence: This is a claim about developmental research supported by a citation.

claim: Evidence for vicarious reinforcement learning has been found whereby reward prediction errors generated by observing the rewards obtained by another have been reported in the striatum.
source: When learning through observation from an agent's actions and outcomes, evidence for a process called vicarious reinforcement learning (RL) has been found whereby reward prediction errors generated by observing the rewards obtained by another as opposed to being received by oneself have been reported in the striatum (Burke et al., 2010; Cooper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about prior neuroscience research supported by citations.

claim: Vicarious RL can only ever work under situations where the rewards being obtained by another agent can be directly observed.
source: However, vicarious RL can only ever work under situations where the rewards being obtained by another agent can be directly observed.
evidence: This is a conceptual limitation of vicarious RL.

claim: Regions of the brain often referred to as the mentalizing network which includes the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex have been implicated in making inferences about the hidden intentions and traits of another agent.
source: In particular, regions of the brain often referred to as the mentalizing network which includes the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) have been implicated in this type of inference (Frith and Frith, 2006; Hampton et al., 2008; Nicolle et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a claim about prior neuroscience research supported by citations.

claim: Posterior superior temporal sulcus and adjacent temporoparietal junction has been found to reflect learning signals about relevant attributes of other individuals' behavior.
source: whereas posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and adjacent temporoparietal junction (TPJ) has been found to reflect learning signals about relevant attributes of other individuals' behavior (Hampton et al., 2008; Behrens et al., 2009; Boorman et al., 2013; Dunne and O'Doherty, 2013).
evidence: This is a claim about prior neuroscience research supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have not addressed the capacity to make inferences about the structure of the environment through observing an agent beyond mentalizing about the intentions/traits of that agent.
source: Yet, these studies have not addressed the capacity to make inferences about the structure of the environment through observing an agent beyond mentalizing about the intentions/traits of that agent him/herself.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: The more successfully an observer can represent the other agent's action-values in dmPFC, the better the observer can utilize these representations to guide their own behavior.
source: These findings suggest that the more successfully an observer can represent the other agent's action-values in dmPFC, the better the observer can utilize these representations to guide their own behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the brain-behavior correlation results.

claim: The observer is not only capable of representing expected values according to the subjective preferences of the observed agent, but when the observer is required to make his/her own choices, the observer can use the same knowledge to compute expected values in own preference space.
source: These findings indicate that the observer is not only capable of representing expected values according to the subjective preferences of the observed agent, but that when the observer is required to make his/her own choices, the observer can use the same knowledge to compute expected values in own preference space, using a network of brain areas involved in social comparisons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: The human brain is capable of performing a variation of inverse reinforcement learning, whereby one learns through observation of actions of other agents with potentially diverging preferences.
source: In conclusion, here we showed that the human brain is capable of performing a variation of inverse reinforcement learning, whereby one learns through observation of actions of other agents with potentially diverging preferences.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: By inferring the distribution of outcomes over available actions from the choices of the agent, participants successfully guided their own choices on the same task.
source: By inferring the distribution of outcomes over available actions from the choices of the agent, participants successfully guided their own choices on the same task.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: A network of regions in the brain, especially areas traditionally implicated in mentalizing and theory of mind, such as the TPJ, pSTS and anterior dmPFC, appear to play a direct role in inverse RL.
source: We found evidence that a network of regions in the brain, especially areas traditionally implicated in mentalizing and theory of mind, such as the TPJ, pSTS and anterior dmPFC, appear to play a direct role in inverse RL.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings.

claim: Neural signals in dmPFC implied that participants learned by representing action values in agent preference space, not their own.
source: Importantly, neural signals in dmPFC implied that participants learned by representing action values in agent preference space, not their own, suggesting that their inference was abstract (i.e., disconnected from their own involvement) rather than concrete (i.e., directly relevant to their own choice situation).
evidence: This is a summary of the key fMRI finding.

claim: Posterior cortical areas such as the TPJ and adjacent pSTS were found to be especially involved in updating and learning about agent preferences and expectations irrespective of the specifics of the task participants had to fulfill themselves.
source: Posterior cortical areas such as the TPJ and adjacent pSTS were found to be especially involved in updating and learning about agent preferences and expectations irrespective of the specifics of the task participants had to fulfill themselves.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Rostral dmPFC was particularly involved in representing agents' valuations in a way that these could eventually be used to guide own choices.
source: By contrast, rostral dmPFC was particularly involved in representing agents' valuations in a way that these could eventually be used to guide own choices.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: 50 participants were recruited between the ages of 18 and 40.
source: 50 participants were recruited between the ages of 18 and 40 (mean: 27.1 years ± 4.9, 25 female).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Seven participants were excluded due to excessive head motion or technical difficulties during scanning.
source: We excluded seven participants due to excessive head motion or technical difficulties during scanning (leaving 23 male, 20 female).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria and final sample.

claim: The included participants did not exhibit scan to scan movements of greater than one voxel within a session.
source: The included participants did not exhibit scan to scan movements of greater than one voxel within a session.
evidence: This describes the quality control criteria for fMRI data.

claim: All participants received $60 compensation.
source: All participants received $60 compensation, and were asked to remain for 30 min after the end of the MRI sessions, where they were allowed to consume the won food item ad libitum.
evidence: This describes the compensation procedure.

claim: A debrief after the experiment revealed that all participants thought they were observing real agents.
source: A debrief after the experiment revealed that all participants thought they were observing real agents.
evidence: This is a result from the post-experiment debrief.

claim: The observational learning phase totaled 150 trials: 100 observations and 50 self-choices.
source: This phase of the experiment totaled 150 trials: 100 observations and 50 self-choices.
evidence: This describes the trial structure of the experiment.

claim: The agent was implemented as a softmax learner with a fixed learning rate and temperature.
source: In this phase, the agent was implemented as a softmax learner, which was simulated for each session with a fixed learning rate and temperature.
evidence: This describes the computational model used to generate agent behavior.

claim: The simulated agent exhibited the same behavioral characteristics in the similar and dissimilar condition.
source: Thus, the simulated agent exhibited the same behavioral characteristics in the similar and dissimilar condition.
evidence: This describes a control feature of the experimental design.

claim: fMRI images were collected using a 3T Siemens Trio scanner with a 32-channel radio frequency coil.
source: The fMRI images were collected using a 3T Siemens Trio scanner located at the Caltech Brain Imaging Center (Pasadena, CA) with a 32-channel radio frequency coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Forty-four axial slices were acquired in oblique orientation of 30 degrees to the anterior commissure–posterior commissure line.
source: Forty-four axial slices were acquired in oblique orientation of 30 degrees to the anterior commissure–posterior commissure line, with a repetition time (TR) of 2780 ms, TE of 30 ms, 80° flip angle, 3 mm isotropic resolution, 192 mm × 192 mm field of view.
evidence: This describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: All image analyses were performed using SPM12.
source: All image analyses were performed using SPM12 (rev. 6906; http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm, RRID:SCR_007037), following a standard preprocessing pipeline.
evidence: This describes the software used for fMRI analysis.

claim: The fMRI results depicted in the main figures are based on an uncorrected threshold of p=0.001 combined with an FWE-corrected cluster threshold of p=0.05.
source: The fMRI results depicted in the main figures are based on an uncorrected threshold of p=0.001 (which is illustrated as z>3.3 in the figures) combined with an FWE-corrected cluster threshold of p=0.05 (here, k = 114).
evidence: This describes the statistical thresholding used for fMRI results.

claim: All regression estimates from Figure 3 and Figure 4 were conducted based on a leave-one-out procedure to avoid non-independence bias.
source: All regression estimates from Figure 3 and Figure 4 were conducted based on a leave-one-out procedure (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009) to avoid non-independence bias.
evidence: This describes the method used to extract parameter estimates.

claim: The full anonymized dataset from this study is available in the NDAR data repository under the collection ID 2417.
source: The full anonymized dataset from this study is available in the NDAR data repository https://ndar.nih.gov/ under the collection ID 2417.
evidence: This describes data availability.

claim: The fMRI activation maps are available at neurovault.
source: The fMRI activation maps are available at neurovault (http://neurovault.org/collections/ZZHNHAJU/).
evidence: This describes data availability.
